title: The Raising Standards Lead
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles takes aim at the secondary school role of Raising Standards Lead, tracing it back to the PIXL era of easy qualifications, early entry and league table gaming, and argues that the job still carries the accounting logic of that period. In the typical version he describes, the RSL pulls failing students out of option subjects, narrows the curriculum to English and maths, sorts pupils into winnables and unwinnables, and holds heads of department to account after every assessment. His counter proposal is to swap the language of standards for the language of learning and to rebuild the role around curriculum and assessment design rather than intervention. That means identifying the exam questions and assessment objectives that actually carry the marks, predicting likely questions and giving students graded model answers to deconstruct, building a long term memory curriculum of core knowledge, and finishing the year 11 curriculum by March. He also pushes hard against fortnight long mocks, proposing rolling subject windows of in class exam practice plus regular knowledge tests, with AI marking used to diagnose what a cohort is missing. The through line is that a raising standards role which does not improve the curriculum is not leadership at all but administration.
points: Salles traces the RSL role to PIXL's loophole hunting in 2012 to 2016 and argues the accountability habits of that era still shape the job.
He claims questions 4 and 5 account for over 72 percent of the English language grade, so mocks should drill only those rather than cycling through every paper.
He singles out AO6, worth 32 of 160 marks, as the most valuable thing an English department teaches and asks whether schools have an AO6 curriculum at all.
He wants the year 11 curriculum finished by March so that revision has 19 months of secured knowledge to draw on rather than fresh teaching to catch up.
He proposes replacing two week mock windows with rotating subject slots of in class exam practice, regular knowledge tests and AI generated diagnostics.
quotes: Back in 2012-2016, I thought PIXL was to education what ‘empowered’ teenage models are to Only Fans - they saw a gap in the market, exploited it and left only emptiness behind.

But it still carries with it traces of those early days of Ponzi schemes, of robbing Peter to pay Paul, of making every student take a qualification they didn’t need, so the school would be worse but look better in a league table.
What if we took away the language of accountability - standards - and replaced it with the language of education - learning?
If you are still teaching in March, what hope do students have of remembering what you taught for the previous 19 months?
If students know more, they will find revision easier and less time consuming, and get higher grades with less effort.
AO6 is literally the most important thing you teach. Only, do you teach it? Do you have an AO6 curriculum?
There is little value in huge mocks, with students out of the curriculum for 2 weeks.
If you aren’t scaling your teachers by improving the curriculum, you are not leading a team, you are just managing resources, email, and admin.
